title: Noraldim Kamis
content: Noraldim Kamis - software engineer. Projects, papers and articles on cloud, computer vision, full-stack web and Linux infrastructure. About Me Hi, I am Noraldim Kamis — a software engineer based in Bilecik, Türkiye, with a B.Sc. in Computer Engineering from Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University. I build software end-to-end: the interface people touch, the services behind it, and the Linux and container infrastructure it runs on. Right now I work at Baynal Group , where I delivered the Health Education Platform for the Bilecik Provincial Health Directorate under a government contract — web application and companion mobile app, both built end-to-end. Before that I spent a year as a network engineer at my university, running campus-wide servers, DNS and switching, and moving internal services onto Docker and Kubernetes. My capstone project sits at the other end of the range: a computer-vision pipeline that segments satellite imagery to find buildable land, then plans a city on top of it. That mix — shipping products, running the systems under them, and pushing on the research side — is what I like about this work. Now Software Engineer at Baynal Group, Bilecik — 2026 to present Education B.Sc. Computer Engineering, Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University, 2022 – 2026 Before Network Engineer, Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University (2024 – 2025) · Data Specialist, Dent Spa, Istanbul (2024 – 2025) Recognition TEKNOFEST national finalist — drone-based fire detection, 2023 What I Work With Languages Python, JavaScript (ES6+), PHP, C, C++, Java, SQL, Bash, PowerShell Frontend React, Next.js, HTML5, CSS3, responsive and mobile-first layouts, reusable component architecture, internationalization (i18n) Backend & data REST API design, server-side rendering, Node.js tooling, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, relational data modeling Cloud & DevOps AWS, GCP, Docker, Kubernetes, OpenShift, Ansible, Linux administration & hardening Networking TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, Active Directory, Graylog, switch and server infrastructure AI & ML PyTorch, semantic segmentation (VM-UNet / Vision Mamba, U-Net, DeepLabV3+), LLM integration, pandas Tools Git, Vim, Linux (Ubuntu & Debian) Explore Projects Production platforms, the urban-planning capstone, campus infrastructure, and the smaller systems work in between — with links to the code. Papers Research write-ups: satellite land segmentation and city planning, drone tracking with YOLOv8 and a Kalman filter, radix conversion down to assembly, and plant disease diagnosis. Articles Shorter pieces on Linux, Vim, databases and chatbots — published here, on dev.to, and alongside the repositories they describe. Why Linux? Linux and cloud computing look like separate subjects until you run something real. Most cloud services depend on Linux to run their servers, and distributions like Ubuntu LTS have become the default for a reason: they are stable, predictable, and they get out of the way. Building local labs and local servers is what pulled me toward cloud computing in the first place — and it is still the fastest way I know to find out whether you actually understand a system or only understand the diagram of it. title: ASTRON: Real-Time UAV Detection and Trajectory Prediction with YOLOv8 and a Kalman Filter
content: A custom YOLOv8 drone detector paired with a constant-velocity Kalman filter. The paper covers the theory, every implementation choice and what each one costs in pixels. Research article · 2024 · 16 pages · English ASTRON: Real-Time UAV Detection and Trajectory Prediction with YOLOv8 and a Kalman Filter What it is about Detecting a drone in a video tells you where it is . Predicting where it will be is what lets a camera, a gimbal or an interceptor follow it. ASTRON is a compact real-time system that couples a YOLOv8 detector with a discrete-time Kalman filter built on OpenCV. The paper is a complete, self-contained account of it, from the network architecture to the filter maths to simulations that drive the actual OpenCV filter. 0.956 mAP@0.5 of the custom uav detector 3.0 M detector parameters 5.7 px forecast error after tuning (down from 10.7) 45× error reduction from a measurement gate What the paper covers The YOLOv8 architecture, and a single-class uav detector trained for 100 epochs on the IHA Nesne Tespit dataset: precision 0.927, recall 0.905, mAP@0.5:0.95 of 0.582. The Kalman filter derived from first principles and specialised to ASTRON’s four-state constant-velocity model. What every implementation choice really does: OpenCV’s default covariances (Q = R = I, P 0 = 0), the correct-then-predict call order that turns the output into a one-step-ahead forecast, and the coupling with a colour-threshold localiser. A proof that the filter settles into a steady-state α–β tracker with α = 0.822 and β = 0.422. Reproducible experiments on straight-line motion, a circular manoeuvre and missed detections. The default tuning amplifies detector noise, and a noise ratio r/q ≈ 100 fixes it. When the target is missed, the localiser reports the image origin, which can drag the prediction by more than 500 px. A simple gate cuts that to 11 px. A concrete roadmap from ASTRON to a full tracking-by-detection system. YOLOv8 Kalman Filter Object Tracking OpenCV State Estimation

title: From Decimal Digits to Binary Bits: Radix Conversion in C, IA-32 and x86-64
content: One conversion algorithm followed all the way down: the mathematics, the C code, the machine code GCC emits for two architectures, and a web front-end. Computer architecture · 2024 – 2025 · 6 pages · English From Decimal Digits to Binary Bits: Radix Conversion in C, IA-32 and x86-64 What it is about Every number a person types is decimal, and every number a processor stores is binary. The boundary between the two is where bugs like 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 come from. This paper takes the BM_Architecture course project, which converts BCD-style decimal inputs such as 532.13022 into binary, and follows it from the mathematics to the machine code to the browser. 2 −10 worst-case error of the C program (exact for dyadic fractions) 25–55 fractional bits printed by the web converter 2 instruction sets compared side by side 6 robustness defects found and characterised What the paper covers The two classical algorithms, repeated division for the integer part and repeated doubling for the fraction, formalised with proofs of correctness, termination and the truncation-error bound ε < 2 −n . A line-by-line walk through the C implementation. The machine code GCC 12.2 produces for both targets: IA-32’s stack-based x87 FPU and cdecl calling convention versus the SSE2 register file and System V AMD64 ABI of x86-64. Every compiler idiom is explained. The HTML/JavaScript front-end: a BCD number generator, and a 16-bit sign-magnitude binary calculator whose loop length depends on the unit in the last place of an IEEE-754 double. An experimental evaluation, six robustness defects (negative inputs, int overflow, malformed input and more), and an exact, integer-only conversion routine that removes all floating-point error. C IA-32 x86-64 IEEE 754 Computer Architecture

title: Automated Diagnosis of Plant Leaf Diseases Using Machine Learning
content: An image-processing pipeline for recognising leaf diseases, trained on phone photos from a home garden and on the PlantVillage dataset. Image processing · 2025 · 15 pages · Turkish Automated Diagnosis of Plant Leaf Diseases Using Machine Learning What it is about Can a neural network tell a healthy leaf from a sick one? This project builds the whole pipeline from scratch on two very different sources. One is photos taken with a phone in the author’s own garden, under changing light and on natural backgrounds. The other is the clean, labelled PlantVillage dataset from Kaggle. The report walks through every step, from the raw photo to the predicted class. 2 datasets: home garden and PlantVillage 128×128 normalised grayscale input 4 hand-crafted features per region of interest ≈60% test accuracy What the paper covers Image collection and preprocessing: resizing to a fixed 128×128, grayscale conversion and normalisation to [0, 1]. Labelling and one-hot encoding of disease classes, and how an image becomes a NumPy matrix the model can read. Region-of-interest selection and feature extraction: pixel mean and variance, Canny edge density, colour histogram and contour count. Training a multi-layer neural network and testing it on images it has never seen. An honest observation: the model does better on the standardised PlantVillage images than on the garden photos, because real-world lighting and image quality vary much more. title: AI-Assisted Plant Disease Detection and Decision Support Platform
content: A TÜBİTAK 2209-A project: a software platform that watches live drone or camera video, finds each leaf, names its disease and suggests what the farmer should do. TÜBİTAK 2209-A research project · 2025 – 2026 · 4 pages · Turkish AI-Assisted Plant Disease Detection and Decision Support Platform What it is about Plant diseases are usually noticed too late, and checking large fields by eye or in a lab is slow and expensive. This TÜBİTAK 2209-A project, supervised by Dr. Ayşenur Türkmen at Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University, builds a fully software-based platform that works on continuous video instead of single photos. It finds each leaf, names the disease, records it once, and turns the result into treatment advice. It works with any drone, field camera or Raspberry Pi, and any trained model can be swapped in while it runs. 2 stages: YOLO finds the leaf, a CNN / ViT names the disease 900 → 1 duplicate records per leaf, cut by track-based de-duplication 38 disease classes in the integrated PlantVillage classifier 0 location or personal data stored What the paper covers An API-first architecture on Python, FastAPI, Ultralytics, PyTorch, OpenCV and SQLite. The web interface, a future mobile app and edge devices all share one REST interface, and inference never runs inside a request handler. Source abstraction: screen capture (for a drone app mirrored to a PC), video files, USB/CSI cameras and RTSP streams can be switched at runtime without stopping the pipeline. Decoupled capture and inference through a single latest-frame slot instead of a queue. Old frames are dropped, so latency never builds up and the system adapts itself to the hardware it runs on. Two-stage detection: YOLO (v8/11) locates each leaf and ByteTrack gives it an ID, then a MobileNetV2 or ViT classifier names the disease on the crop. De-duplication: one diseased leaf in view for 30 s at 30 FPS would create about 900 identical records. Persistent track IDs, a per-ID cool-down, a confidence threshold and a minimum box area cut that to one. A decision-support engine that maps each disease to its risk, symptoms, treatment and a natural remedy. A model registry hot-swaps any uploaded .pt model, with a staged path from ready-made models to fully custom ones. Raspberry Pi edge node in two modes: stream video to a GPU server, or run a lightweight YOLO11n on the Pi and send only detections, which saves bandwidth. An honest baseline (Phase 0): the untrained system identified the plant species correctly but forced out-of-scope plants into the nearest disease class with up to 0.91 confidence. High confidence is not correctness, and this finding justifies training on field data with an “unknown” class. TÜBİTAK 2209-A YOLO ByteTrack FastAPI Raspberry Pi Edge AI

title: Land Segmentation and Smart-City Planning from Satellite Imagery
content: Finding land that is free to build on in Sentinel-2 imagery with seven deep segmentation models, then laying out a whole district on it automatically. Senior capstone · 2025 · 9 pages · English Land Segmentation and Smart-City Planning from Satellite Imagery What it is about Every new district starts with the same question: where is there land that can be built on? Today that is still answered by hand, from cadastral records and photo-interpretation. Urban-Planner answers it end-to-end. It segments open land in 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery with deep encoder–decoder networks, then hands the mask to a rule-based planner that places a full district (houses, apartments, shops, schools, a hospital, a stadium) with no overlaps. 0.942 overall score, DeepLabV3+ with ResNet-101 0.938 best Dice score (U-Net, ResNet-101) 0.725 Dice of a trivial “all land” baseline 84% of tiles fit the full 236-building plan What the paper covers Turning the 2,433 patches of the PASTIS benchmark into a binary open land vs. background target (60.1% positive pixels), and analysing the resulting dataset. Seven models compared under one metric suite: U-Net with ResNet-34, ResNet-101 and VGG-16 encoders, and DeepLabV3+ with ResNet-50, ResNet-101, Xception and EfficientNet-B5. Each one is described down to the layer its features are tapped from. The result: DeepLabV3+ beats U-Net and is more robust to configuration, and ResNet-101 is the best encoder in both families. The layer-level analysis shows that the Xception and EfficientNet-B5 taps sit one stride level higher than intended. An honest reading of the protocol. The reported scores are computed on images seen during training, so they are upper bounds, and the paper proposes a fold-based protocol to fix that. A formal, reproducible version of the smart-city planner. When a tile fails, it is because the land is too fragmented , not because there is too little of it. Semantic Segmentation U-Net DeepLabV3+ Sentinel-2 Urban Planning

title: Building a Telegram Chatbot from My Chat History
content: Building a Telegram bot that answers in my own voice: cleaning raw chat exports with Python, storing them in PostgreSQL with UTF-8, and replying through the Telegram Bot API. Contents Building a Telegram Chatbot from My Chat History Noraldim Kamis 2023-02-11 734 words 4 minutes Contents Also published on dev.to . Data Cleaning You can clean with basic cleaning commands in python using ‘open’ to open specific files and associate it with a variable and use ‘replace ’ to replace the element. In our case we just need to clean. Finally, we can use append to do the work. import re rmnum = re.compile(r'/d+') one = [] with open("C:\\THINGS\\githup project\\meshochat.txt", 'r', encoding= "utf-8") as mesho: for line in mesho: rm = line.replace('/','').replace(':','').replace('AM','').replace('PM','') .replace('-','').replace(',','').replace(' ','').replace('ميشووو','ques ') .replace('Nõr','ans ') one.append(rm) to delete the changing number in the date u can use re.compile(r’\d+’) to delete any number from chat after cleaning the chat you will start to sort data in the table and here you need to learn RELATIONAL DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM in order to handle the data and store them. in my case, I use PostgreSQL to handle chat log data and there are some important things you must get hands-on : Storing the Data in PostgreSQL 1- IF you handle your data with PostgreSQL you have to realize that by default it only accepts ASCII characters: 2- you need to use the “UTF-8” encoding method to avoid any error especially if you use a character out site ASCII list like Arabic characters . . NOTE USE : _CREATE DATABASE bot WITH ENCODING'UTF8_' 3- need to know how to handle data using psycopg2 or any other library to store and customize data in an effective way import psycopg2 conect = psycopg2.connect( host = "localhost", database = "time", user = "postgres", password = "timezone" ) cur = conect.cursor() cur.execute("INSERT INTO static(name, last_name, gender, email) VALUES('ONE','SALIH','FEMEAL','Eada@gmail.com');") cur.execute("SELECT * FROM static;") rows = cur.fetchall() # use for loop to print ever line you spasify for line in rows: print(f"{line[0]} {line[1]} {line[2]} {line[3]} {line[4]}") conect.commit() cur.close() conect.close() Git and GitHub After storing the data in CSV or TSV format you can use Git to upload your data to GitHub and there are some commands that will help you do that: “git init " and “git add .” These two commands are important the first is to create the git hidden file to initialize the project and the second one is to add an initialized folders to git file and finally you can use git commit to commit your initialization and git push to upload to GitHub in this way avoid any uploading error happening when you use drag and drop method. After uploading the tsv file opens it in row form and copies the link this link will be the database for the chatbox bot. From now on you can use any language to code the bot. In my case I use python because again I have many ways to handle data and here using pandas this tool gives you a mighty hand on accessing your data and distributing them in a way that serves your needs . The actual bot is divided into four parts. The first part just defines the database and bot api . from typing import Counter import requests import pandas as pd resp = [ "Sorry ","have a nice day"] dburl = "DATABASElink.tsv" url = "botapi/" counter = 0 Responding to Users the second part is reading the user message offset is the message id or “update_id” each message has an unique id and here you need to extract some information from json format like message and user id that change automatically . def read(offset): para = { "offset" : offset } req = requests.get(url + "getUpdates", data = para) data = req.json() print(data) for result in data["result"]: send(result) if data["result"]: return data["result"][-1]["update_id"] + 1 The third part is to process input given by the user if there is any capital letter it will make it small and so on and if there is any message that not exist in the database it will give auto response from a list created privily in this case “resp”. def out(message): global counter answer = df.loc[df['qus'].str.lower()== message.lower()] if not answer.empty: answer = answer.iloc[0]['ans'] return answer else: counter = (counter + 1) % len(resp) return resp[counter] the final part is sending message part here there is just a simple parameter take sends a message to the id that stores priestly from a list in the database. def send(result): text = result["message"]["text"] answer = out(text) parameter = { "chat_id" : result["message"]["chat"]["id"], "text" : answer , "reply_to_message_id" : None } req = requests.get(url + "sendMessage", data = parameter) print(req.text) offset = 0 Updated on 2023-02-11 All articles | Home Exploring the Power and Impact of Linux

title: File Handling in C++
content: File handling in C++ with fstream: opening, writing, reading, appending and closing files, checking for end-of-file, and handling errors. Contents File Handling in C++ Noraldim Kamis 2023-05-31 598 words 3 minutes Contents File Handling in C++ File handling in C++ refers to the process of accessing files, reading data from them, writing data to them, creating, deleting, or modifying files. File operations are performed using a set of functions and classes provided by the standard library in C++, specifically the <fstream> header file. File handling typically involves the following steps: 1. Opening a File To perform operations on a file, an object of type std::fstream is created. This object can be used for reading, writing, or both, depending on the opening mode ( std::ios::in , std::ios::out , std::ios::app , etc.) specified while opening the file. #include <fstream> std :: fstream file; file.open( "file.txt" , std :: ios :: out); // Open file in write mode 2. Writing Data to a File To write data to an open file, the << operator or the write() function is used. file << "Hello, writing to a file! \n " ; 3. Reading Data from a File To read data from an open file, the >> operator or the read() function is used. std :: string line; std :: getline(file, line); // Read a line from the file std :: cout << "Read line: " << line << std :: endl; 4. Closing a File It is important to close a file once it is no longer needed. This releases the associated memory resources. file.close(); // Close the file During file handling, it is important to handle errors and handle them appropriately if they occur. File opening, writing, or reading operations can fail, leading to unexpected termination of the program. Therefore, proper error checking and handling should be performed. if ( ! file) { std :: cerr << "File opening error!" << std :: endl; // Perform necessary actions to handle the error } The <fstream> header file in C++ provides various other functions and details related to file handling. Operations like opening files in binary or text mode, positioning within a file, deleting or renaming files can also be performed. For more detailed functionality and options, refer to the documentation and references for the C++ standard library. Examples 1. Writing Data to a File #include <fstream> int main () { std :: ofstream file( "data.txt" ); // Open file for writing if (file.is_open()) { file << "Hello, File Handling!" << std :: endl; file << "This is another line." << std :: endl; file.close(); // Close the file std :: cout << "Data written to file successfully." << std :: endl; } else { std :: cerr << "Failed to open the file." << std :: endl; } return 0 ; } 2. Reading Data from a File #include <fstream> int main () { std :: ifstream file( "data.txt" ); // Open file for reading if (file.is_open()) { std :: string line; while (std :: getline(file, line)) { std :: cout << line << std :: endl; } file.close(); // Close the file } else { std :: cerr << "Failed to open the file." << std :: endl; } return 0 ; } 3. Appending Data to a File #include <fstream> int main () { std :: ofstream file( "data.txt" , std :: ios :: app); // Open file in append mode if (file.is_open()) { file << "This line will be appended." << std :: endl; file.close(); // Close the file std :: cout << "Data appended to file successfully." << std :: endl; } else { std :: cerr << "Failed to open the file." << std :: endl; } return 0 ; } Checking End - of - File (EOF) : 4. Checking End-of-File (EOF) #include <fstream> int main () { std :: ifstream file( "data.txt" ); // Open file for reading if (file.is_open()) { std :: string line; while ( ! file.eof()) { std :: getline(file, line); if ( ! file.eof()) { std :: cout << line << std :: endl; } } file.close(); // Close the file } else { std :: cerr << "Failed to open the file." << std :: endl; } return 0 ; } These examples demonstrate different file handling operations such as writing, reading, appending, and checking the end-of-file. Feel free to modify them or experiment with your own file handling scenarios. Updated on 2023-05-31 All articles | Home Why Vim is an Efficient Text Editor

title: Exploring the Power and Impact of Linux
content: Why Linux runs so much of the world: its stability under heavy workloads, the security of open source, and its reach from servers and the cloud to Android and IoT. Contents Exploring the Power and Impact of Linux Noraldim Kamis 2023-03-23 299 words 2 minutes Contents 1. Stability: Empowering High Workloads Linux’s unwavering stability sets it apart as a robust and reliable open-source operating system. Its ability to handle high workloads without crashes or performance degradation has made it a preferred choice for critical infrastructure, particularly servers. With Linux, uninterrupted service and optimal uptime are ensured, making it an ideal solution for mission-critical environments. 2. Security: Open-Source Strength Linux’s security features are highly regarded, stemming from its open-source nature. The transparency of the operating system allows for comprehensive security audits and swift resolution of vulnerabilities. The extensive community of security experts actively contributes to identifying and addressing potential security issues, resulting in a highly secure environment. As a result, Linux-based systems are widely embraced in settings where data protection is of paramount importance. 3. Impact on the Computing Landscape Linux has made a profound impact on the world of computing, permeating a wide array of devices and systems. It serves as the backbone of a substantial portion of the internet, powering web servers, cloud infrastructure, and data centers. The efficiency and scalability of Linux also make it prevalent in embedded systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Additionally, the global smartphone market is dominated by the Android operating system, which is based on the Linux kernel. Linux’s versatility and adaptability have solidified its position as a driving force in shaping the modern computing landscape. Overall By embracing stability, security, and adaptability, Linux has emerged as a powerful and influential open-source operating system. Its ability to handle high workloads, coupled with its robust security framework, has propelled its adoption in critical infrastructures. Furthermore, Linux’s impact extends to diverse domains, from powering the internet to enabling embedded systems and smartphone dominance. With its rich history and continued innovation, Linux continues to redefine the boundaries of computing excellence. title: Why Vim is an Efficient Text Editor
content: Why Vim is worth learning: modal editing, language support, handling very large files, long-term speed, and GVim for people who prefer a graphical interface. Contents Why Vim is an Efficient Text Editor Noraldim Kamis 2023-04-17 378 words 2 minutes Contents 1. Modal Editing System: Enhancing Productivity One of the key features of Vim is its modal editing system. With different modes at the users’ disposal, they can efficiently perform various tasks. The two primary modes, command mode and insert mode, offer distinct functionalities. Command mode facilitates navigation, searching, and executing commands, while insert mode is dedicated to text insertion and editing. This modal approach empowers users to achieve quick and precise editing, making Vim a highly efficient tool. 2. Language Support and Advanced Features Vim provides extensive support for numerous programming languages. It offers essential features like syntax highlighting, code folding, and indentation, aiding developers in writing clean and organized code. Vim’s powerful search and replace functionality enables complex text transformations with ease. The ability to work with split windows further enhances productivity, allowing simultaneous work on multiple files, facilitating code comparison and reference to documentation. 3. Handling Large Files with Ease Vim excels at efficiently handling large files, including substantial codebases and log files. Its optimized editing operations and efficient memory usage contribute to its seamless performance. Users can swiftly navigate through files using shortcuts and commands, making it an ideal choice for tasks such as code refactoring or log analysis. 4. Mastery and Proficiency: Long-Term Benefits While Vim has a reputation for a steep learning curve, investing time in learning Vim yields significant long-term advantages. Proficient Vim users can rapidly edit text and perform complex editing tasks efficiently. The key-based navigation and editing commands become second nature, enabling users to work with remarkable speed and precision. 5. Graphical Interface with GVim Apart from the command-line interface, Vim also offers a graphical version called GVim. GVim retains all the features and capabilities of the command-line version but provides a more familiar user interface with menus and toolbar icons. This graphical interface enhances accessibility and convenience for users who prefer a visual approach to text editing. Summary Vim’s modal editing system, language support, advanced features, efficient handling of large files, and the potential for mastery make it a highly efficient text editor. Users who invest time in learning Vim can unlock its full potential and reap the benefits of rapid and precise text editing. The availability of GVim as a graphical alternative further expands the usability of Vim, catering to diverse user preferences. title: Projects
content: Projects by Noraldim Kamis: Madaries multi-tenant school SaaS, Elsiraj currency-exchange marketplace, a government healthcare education platform, an AI urban planner from satellite imagery, and a TEKNOFEST-finalist fire-detection drone. Projects Software I have designed, built and shipped: production platforms used every day by schools, merchants and healthcare staff, research in computer vision, and the infrastructure underneath it all. 3 production platforms live, used by schools, merchants and healthcare staff 120+ active users on a government health-education platform I delivered 5 research papers, including a TÜBİTAK 2209-A project Finalist at TEKNOFEST, Türkiye’s national technology competition All Web & product AI & research Cloud & infrastructure Systems & tools Featured work 2025 · Multi-tenant SaaS · Web + Android Madaries — School Management Platform One platform that runs many schools: student records, grades, attendance, timetables, finance and reports, with every school’s data kept completely separate. Multi-tenant architecture on Next.js and PostgreSQL : many schools run from a single deployment with per-school data isolation. Eight permission-scoped roles across student records, grading, attendance, timetabling and finance. Redis caching in front of PostgreSQL keeps response times steady under concurrent load. Two-factor authentication, full activity logging and automated backups. Released in Arabic and English (RTL) on the web and Google Play . Next.js PostgreSQL Redis Multi-tenancy RBAC 2FA Arabic / RTL 2026 · Fintech marketplace Elsiraj — Currency-Exchange Marketplace A digital intermediary between customers and verified currency merchants: a clear order, evidence kept on record, and a full history from the first step to the money arriving. Merchant storefronts publish live rates and limits before anyone places an order. Orders are created against a locked-in rate , so the customer sees the applied rate and exact payout before confirming. Payment-proof uploads and merchant verification, with an auditable history for every transaction. One customer account across every merchant. Bilingual Arabic / English with full right-to-left support, installable as a PWA . Next.js PostgreSQL PWA Fintech Arabic / RTL i18n 2026 · Baynal Group · Government contract SEP — National Healthcare Education Platform A training platform delivered for the Bilecik Provincial Health Directorate . Healthcare staff take mandatory and elective trainings, earn digital certificates and track their progress. Built the web application , its REST APIs and the companion cross-platform mobile app end-to-end. Online trainings, instant digital certificates, real-time progress reporting and mobile notifications. Sign-in by email or Turkish ID number, with Turkish and English throughout. In production: the live site reports 120+ active users , 40+ trainings and 6 departments. React Next.js REST API Mobile app i18n 2025 – 2026 · Senior capstone · Computer vision AI-Driven Urban Planner From satellite pixels to a city plan. Deep segmentation finds land that is free to build on, then an automated planner lays out a whole district on top of it. Segments 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery. Seven U-Net and DeepLabV3+ models are compared on a binary open-land dataset derived from PASTIS. The best model (DeepLabV3+ with ResNet-101) reaches a 0.942 overall score and 0.937 Dice, well above the 0.725 of a trivial baseline. A rule-based, conflict-free planner places hospitals, stadiums, malls, apartments and houses. A 236-building plan fits completely on 84% of tiles. Results are rendered as an interactive 3D web visualization. Python TensorFlow / Keras U-Net DeepLabV3+ Sentinel-2 JavaScript 2023 · TEKNOFEST national finalist Drone-Based Fire Detection System A drone that finds fires in the field and tells the ground team exactly where they are. A drone-mounted system that detects fire from the air . Streams real-time imagery with GPS coordinates to a ground control station. Advanced to the national finals of TEKNOFEST , Türkiye’s largest aerospace and technology competition.
